rule.title: WMIC Unquoted Services Path Lookup - PowerShell
rule.author: Nasreddine Bencherchali (Nextron Systems)

es.summary: Un script block de PowerShell consultó la clase WMI Win32_Service con Get-WmiObject o gwmi y pidió Name, DisplayName, PathName y StartMode. Este patrón se usa con frecuencia para buscar servicios con rutas sin comillas.
es.what_it_detects: Eventos 4104 de Script Block Logging en los que ScriptBlockText contiene 'Get-WmiObject ' o 'gwmi ', ' Win32_Service ' y las propiedades Name, DisplayName, PathName y StartMode. Es la consulta típica de scripts de enumeración como JAWS o redsnarf.
es.why_it_matters: Usa WMI para hacer reconocimiento (ATT&CK T1047). Si un servicio tiene una ruta sin comillas que contiene espacios, un atacante con permiso de escritura en una carpeta intermedia puede colocar ahí un ejecutable que el servicio iniciará como SYSTEM.
triage_steps: Lea el ScriptBlockText completo. Si el script llegó en varios fragmentos, reconstrúyalo con ScriptBlockId, MessageNumber y MessageTotal, y busque filtros como -notlike '"*' o StartMode Auto.
Revise el campo Path y el usuario del evento. Un script en Temp, Downloads o ejecutado desde memoria es más sospechoso que uno de administración conocido.
Identifique el proceso padre de powershell.exe con Sysmon 1 o 4688 en el mismo host, ±15 minutos: Office, cmd, wmiprvse o un agente remoto.
En la misma ventana, busque otros comandos de enumeración: whoami /priv, icacls, accesschk, sc qc o herramientas como PowerUp o winPEAS.
Busque escrituras posteriores de ejecutables en rutas intermedias, por ejemplo C:\Program.exe o carpetas de Program Files, y eventos 7045 o 4697 de servicios nuevos o modificados.
Compruebe si hay alertas anteriores del mismo usuario o host y si existe una prueba de penetración o una auditoría autorizada en curso.
false_positives: Scripts de inventario o de hardening que buscan rutas sin comillas para corregirlas.
Escáneres de vulnerabilidades o herramientas de cumplimiento que lanzan esta consulta por PowerShell.
Pruebas de penetración o ejercicios de red team autorizados.
response_steps: Confirme con el dueño del usuario o del host si la actividad era legítima y estaba autorizada.
Si no lo era, aísle el endpoint y preserve los registros de PowerShell y el script original.
Cambie de inmediato las credenciales de la cuenta afectada si hay indicios de compromiso.
Después de validarlo, elimine los ejecutables plantados y revierta los cambios en servicios.
Corrija las rutas sin comillas poniéndolas entre comillas y restrinja la escritura en las carpetas intermedias.
es.severity_rationale: La severidad es media porque esto es reconocimiento sin daño directo, aunque suele ser el paso previo a una escalada de privilegios local.

en.summary: A PowerShell script block queried the WMI class Win32_Service through Get-WmiObject or gwmi and asked for Name, DisplayName, PathName and StartMode. This pattern is commonly used to find services with unquoted paths.
en.what_it_detects: Script Block Logging events (4104) where ScriptBlockText contains 'Get-WmiObject ' or 'gwmi ', ' Win32_Service ', and the properties Name, DisplayName, PathName and StartMode. This is the usual query in enumeration scripts such as JAWS or redsnarf.
en.why_it_matters: It uses WMI for reconnaissance (ATT&CK T1047). When a service path has spaces and no quotes, an attacker who can write to a folder along that path can drop an executable that the service will launch as SYSTEM.
triage_steps: Read the full ScriptBlockText. If the script was split, rebuild it with ScriptBlockId, MessageNumber and MessageTotal, and look for filters like -notlike '"*' or StartMode Auto.
Check the Path field and the user on the event. A script in Temp or Downloads, or one run from memory, is more suspicious than a known admin script.
Find the parent of powershell.exe using Sysmon 1 or 4688 on the same host, within ±15 minutes: Office, cmd, wmiprvse or a remote agent.
In the same window, look for other enumeration: whoami /priv, icacls, accesschk, sc qc, or tools such as PowerUp or winPEAS.
Look for executables written afterwards along service paths, such as C:\Program.exe or folders under Program Files, and for 7045 or 4697 events showing new or changed services.
Check for earlier alerts on the same user or host, and whether an authorized pentest or audit is underway.
false_positives: Inventory or hardening scripts that look for unquoted paths so they can be fixed.
Vulnerability scanners or compliance tools that run this query through PowerShell.
Authorized penetration tests or red team exercises.
response_steps: Ask the user or the host owner whether the activity was legitimate and authorized.
If it was not, isolate the endpoint and preserve the PowerShell logs and the original script.
Reset the account's credentials right away if you see signs of compromise.
Once verified, remove any planted executables and revert changes to services.
Fix unquoted service paths by adding quotes, and restrict write access to the folders along those paths.
en.severity_rationale: Severity is medium because this is reconnaissance with no direct impact, though it often comes right before local privilege escalation.

positive.description: JAWS-style one-liner: gwmi lists auto-start services whose paths are unquoted and outside C:\Windows

event.ScriptBlockText: gwmi -class Win32_Service -Property Name, DisplayName, PathName, StartMode | Where {$_.StartMode -eq "Auto" -and $_.PathName -notlike "C:\Windows*" -and $_.PathName -notlike '"*'} | select PathName, DisplayName, Name

positive.description: Get-WmiObject piped to a select of the four service properties

event.ScriptBlockText: Get-WmiObject win32_service | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, PathName, StartMode | Format-Table -AutoSize

negative.description: Admin checks the Spooler service with Get-WmiObject but asks for no PathName, DisplayName or StartMode
Same properties pulled with Get-CimInstance instead of Get-WmiObject or gwmi, so the rule does not match

event.ScriptBlockText: Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, PathName, StartMode | Export-Csv C:\Inventory\services.csv
